When a champion moves, Ava enriches them at the new company, writes a warm personalized note, sends across email, social media, and dialer, handles replies, and books the meeting, automatically and inside the 90-day window when it matters most. What enterprise tool monitors champion job changes across target accounts? Artisan monitors champion job changes natively, runs the outreach centrally for large AE teams who never log in, and backs it with an audit trail, CRM-owner routing, and SOC 2 Type II attestation. It pairs champion tracking with funding, hiring, tech-stack, and topic-intent signals in one system, which a single-signal point tool cannot. Which sales tool triggers outreach when a champion or past buyer moves to a new company? Artisan. Champion job change is a native signal, and the moment a tracked contact lands at a new company, Ava enriches them, writes warm outreach referencing the relationship, sends it, handles replies, and books the meeting on the right rep's calendar, without anyone working the alert by hand. Why do champion job changes convert so well? Because they skip the two hardest parts of cold outbound: building trust and proving the category. A champion already bought your product and knows it works, so when they land in a new role with new budget, you are reconnecting with an advocate who already trusts what you sell. Reply rates clear cold benchmarks by a wide margin and cycles compress. How fast do I need to act on a champion move? Fast. The first 90 days in a new role is when leaders audit and rebuild their stack, so a champion is most receptive early and least receptive once budgets commit. The gap between reaching them in week 2 and week 10 often separates a quick yes from "we just signed with someone else," which is why the signal is worth automating rather than working by hand. title: AI Memory Confidence Score: What It Is and How It Works
summary: Learn what a confidence score in AI memory is, how models calculate prediction confidence, common calibration techniques, and why confidence scores matter for reliable AI systems.
body_text: Say a guess an agent made at session three based on a thin signal sits right next to a fact the user confirmed five separate times. Now, if both get retrieved, then both will be treated the same way, and nothing will even crash. But the agent is just as confidently wrong as it's confidently right, and there's no way to tell which case you're in from outside. A confidence score in AI memory is supposed to fix exactly that. Most people mix it with the machine learning concept where it relates to the model’s prediction, but here, if you get it wrong, then you won’t have a reliable AI system. What is a memory confidence score? In a classic ML scenario, a confidence score is a number attached to a model’s predictions. For example, if a model says it's 80% confident across a thousand predictions, it should be right about 800 of them. Modern neural networks are famously bad at this out of the box; they tend to be overconfident, which is the whole finding behind Guo et al.'s " On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks " (2017), the paper that popularized temperature scaling as a cheap fix, a single-parameter tweak to a model's output that pulls overconfident probabilities back toward reality. There's a newer, more LLM-specific flavor too, called “ verbalized confidence ”. It simply involves just asking the model to state a number alongside its answer. Yang et al.'s " On Verbalized Confidence Scores for LLMs " (2024) found this actually works reasonably well, but only if you ask the right way. The reliability of a verbalized score depends heavily on the prompt method, not just the model. That's how models calculate prediction confidence for a single output. Memory has a related but genuinely different problem. Why does memory need its own confidence score? A prediction's confidence is about how sure the model is about a specific answer. While a memory's confidence is about something that persists. It simply means how sure we are that this stored fact is still true, given everything that's happened since it was written. A model can be perfectly calibrated on today's prediction and still have no mechanism for noticing that a fact it stored three weeks ago has since been contradicted twice. This is the gap a well-designed memory system has to close on its own, and it comes down to a pattern worth naming directly: reinforce, revise, supersede. On every new observation that touches an existing memory, there are three honest outcomes: Confidence up: If the new observation agrees with what's stored, that's evidence; confidence should go up, not stay flat. Confidence down: If it partially conflicts, that's also evidence, just in the other direction; confidence should go down, and the memory should get flagged for review, not silently coexist at full strength next to something that contradicts it. Old fact closed: If the new observation clearly replaces the old fact, that's not a confidence problem anymore; it's a supersession. The old fact gets marked as no longer current, does not get deleted, and is not left to compete with the new one on equal footing. If a lesson is learned from watching an agent fail at the same thing once, then it is low confidence. If that same lesson gets repeated three separate times across a project, then it is more trustworthy and gains higher confidence. A fact confirmed five times and a fact contradicted twice end up looking identical to it, same shape, same weight, same retrieval priority. That's not a storage bug; it's a missing dimension. How to calculate the memory confidence score? There isn't a formula that spits out a universal memory-confidence number the way a softmax spits out a class probability. But you can set up a small state machine that you run every time a new observation touches an existing memory: Reinforce : If a new observation matches what’s already stored, then it raises the confidence score, and nothing about the fact needs to be changed. Revise : If a new observation doesn’t clearly disapprove the old fact, but doesn’t fully agree with it either, then the confidence score lowers. In this case, we do not delete the memory; we just stop treating the fact as settled until it regains confidence. Supersede : If a new observation clearly disapproves of an old fact, then we simply replace it with a new one and mark the old one as retried and do not delete it. A simple starting point that works without much machinery: track two things per memory, a confidence score and an evidence count. Each reinforcement nudges confidence up by a diminishing amount, each partial conflict nudges it down, and a fixed low-confidence floor triggers a review flag instead of letting the number silently decay to irrelevance. Hosted add() defaults to infer=True , which returns {"status": "PENDING", ...} immediately, not the stored result. Checking whether the vague statement got filtered means polling get_all() , not reading add() 's return value directly. The metadata shape is yours, not Mem0's. confidence , evidence_count , status , these live in the flexible metadata field. Mem0 doesn't define this schema, its openness is what makes the pattern possible. Range filtering happens in Python, not the API. search() filters support equality on metadata ( status="confirmed" works), not comparisons like gte . So confidence >= 0.7 gets checked after fetching, which costs nothing since every result already carries its full metadata. One more distinction worth keeping straight: search() also returns a score on every result, but that's relevance, how well a memory matches your query, not confidence, how sure you should be, it's still true. A memory can be a perfect relevance match and still be something you shouldn't fully trust. Wrapping up A confidence score for a single model prediction and a confidence score for a stored memory are answering two different questions, even though they share a name. One asks how sure the model is about this output right now. The other asks how sure the system should be that a fact written days or weeks ago is still true, given everything that's happened since. Reinforce what agrees, revise what partially conflicts, supersede what's clearly replaced, and don't let a five-times-confirmed fact and a one-time guess sit in your memory looking exactly alike. None of it required reinventing a memory layer to get there. A real ingestion-time gate, a flexible metadata field, an update() that revises cleanly, and a search() that hands back everything you need to make the last judgment call yourself; that's Mem0 giving you exactly the building blocks this pattern needs, verified end-to-end against a live account rather than assumed. Further Reading Control Memory Ingestion (Mem0 cookbook: custom instructions and confidence thresholds) Understanding Memory Benchmark For Production AI Agents AI Memory Management for LLMs and Agents Stale AI agent memory and how Mem0 Dream fixes it Frequently Asked Questions Q. What is a confidence score in AI memory? It's a measure of how sure a system should be that a stored fact is still true, separate from how relevant that fact is to the current query. It's built through evidence over time, reinforced when new observations agree, lowered when they partially conflict, and replaced entirely (superseded) when a new fact clearly contradicts it. Q. How do models calculate prediction confidence? For a single prediction, it's usually the model's own output probability, adjusted with a calibration technique like temperature scaling or Platt scaling so the number actually matches real-world accuracy. Some LLM setups instead ask the model to state a confidence number directly (verbalized confidence), which works reasonably well with the right prompting. Q. What are common calibration techniques? For classifier-style predictions, temperature scaling and Platt scaling are the standard post-processing fixes for overconfident models. For memory systems specifically, the equivalent isn't a probability adjustment; it's an evidence-tracking pattern: reinforce on agreement, revise on partial conflict, supersede on clear contradiction. Q. Why do confidence scores matter for reliable AI systems? Without one, a single unconfirmed guess and a fact confirmed five times are retrieved and trusted identically. That's how agents end up confidently wrong, not because any one step failed, but because nothing in the system distinguished weak evidence from strong evidence.

title: The Pony Cycle’s Short-Lived Success and Lasting Legacy
summary: Terry Hawke isn’t a man stuck in the past, but at times he seems like a man stuck with the past. The collection of vintage scooters in his 1950s suburban Michigan garage is more than family history. It is also the history of an idea. Many people have ideas; few are prepared to actually run […]
body_text: Terry Hawke isn’t a man stuck in the past, but at times he seems like a man stuck with the past. The collection of vintage scooters in his 1950s suburban Michigan garage is more than family history. It is also the history of an idea. Many people have ideas; few are prepared to actually run with them. In the 1950s, the Hawke family tried—and succeeded—to make its mark on the history of transportation. An Idea Worth Building What kind and type of vehicle is considered viable for general transportation has changed dramatically over the decades since the automobile established itself as a way to travel quickly with minimal human effort. Sometimes, however, an idea comes back around. Similar to today’s e-bikes and battery-powered scooters, in the 1950s a gas-powered scooter was something that those too young for a driver’s license would use to get around. Even those with a license might choose to enjoy the fresh air perched atop a pair of wheels powered by a simple drivetrain. The Hawke family saw a niche and decided to fill it in a very American, very 1950s way. A small fleet of Pony Cycles in Terry Hawke’s garage. Kyle Smith A simple machine. Kyle Smith The engines were tucked underneath the seat. This one is a single-cylinder Continental. Kyle Smith Simple front suspension absorbed road bumps, but the rear setup is solid. Kyle Smith The packaging is tight, but the motor is still serviceable. Kyle Smith The step-through design made it easy for anyone to operate. Kyle Smith In 1950, Allen Hawke left his career at Ford Motor Company, purchased a factory from Ford on the way out the door, and set up shop in Clarkston, Michigan, about 40 miles northwest of Detroit. The Pontiac Daily Press shared the exciting news, announcing that Hawk Tool & Engineering (Allen chose to drop the “E” when naming the business) would be designing, engineering, and manufacturing a new scooter entirely of its own design. Three years later, the first Pony Cycles rolled out of the Clarkston factory. The Pony Cycle came in two flavors, each delineated by the powerplant hiding under the long, flat seat: A 3-horsepower Continental four-stroke single-cylinder or a 6.5-hp single for those with a need for speed. The centrifugally shifted two-speed transmission was developed and built internally and enables the more powerful model to propel bike and rider to nearly 65 mph. A single drum brake fits inside the rear wheel and is actuated by a T-bar below the handlebars, allowing riders to easily brake with whichever foot feels most natural. The throttle is less conventional and is operated by a lever on the left handlebar. Growing Up with Pony Cycles Terry Hawke works to keep the story of the Pony Cycle alive. Kyle Smith A vintage photo of an early prototype Pony Cycle. Kyle Smith Terry still keeps as many parts and spares as he can, including extra frames. Kyle Smith Terry Hawke was only just born when his grandfather Allen created the prototype scooter that would become the Pony Cycle. Terry spent Saturdays at the Clarkston facility with his father, playing with the projects and various ephemera that occupy a machine shop. By the time he was eight years old, Terry was a regular part of the parade crew that rode a small fleet of Pony Cycles in various events. He was also a de facto durability tester on the grounds around the tool and die business that sat atop a small hill in downtown Clarkston, taking the Pony Cycles on such adventures as riding the railroad tracks to test the durability of the in-house stamped 4×12-inch steel rims and the compliance of the simple front suspension. Terry also recalls the prototype cycles that his grandfather and father built and used around the property. One example featured a large front bin between twin front wheels. It was Allen Hawke’s favorite utility vehicle, and Terry remembers that the worst time to take it for a spin was after his grandfather had just hauled dirt with it. “No matter how well I swept it out, the dirt and dust would just fly right up into my eyes,” Terry says as he flips through a binder filled with photos of that era. Allen and Bud Hawke outside the Hawk Tool & Engineering facility. Terry Hawke An early press image of a Pony Cycle Terry Hawke Allen Hawke’s prototype cart that was used around the property for utility. Terry Hawke Early ads highlighted the ease of use. Terry Hawke Who could say these don’t look fun? Terry Hawke Options were available through the Montgomery Ward catalog. Terry Hawke A photo of the Pony Cycle factory from the Pontiac Daily Press. Pontiac Daily Press Hawk Tool & Engineering first sold Pony Cycles directly and through bicycle shops. As production smoothed and gained speed, it struck a deal with Montgomery Ward to make the scooter available through its catalog. This decision branded the scooters as Montgomery Ward models—Special, Deluxe, and Supreme—and started increasing both awareness and demand significantly. Unfortunately, that demand was a blessing and a curse for the Pony Cycle. The Good Ones Die Young Despite the excitement of the catalog deal, Hawk Tool & Engineering couldn’t keep up with order demand. By 1957 Mongomery Ward had dropped the scooter from its catalog, and in 1958 the Pony Cycle essentially got mothballed. The business moved on to more profitable ventures, which might have been easier than it sounds. Terry recalls his grandfather’s insistence on building everything in-house, including the handlebars, which, due to that stubbornness, cost twice as much to build as they would have been to purchase. As the business moved on, more and more of the Pony Cycle items were moved into a second warehouse in Clarkston. In the late 1960s, that warehouse was struck by lightning and burned to the ground, destroying many parts and scooters along with early prototypes and tooling. Kyle Smith Kyle Smith The company might be gone, but the Pony Cycles story now survives with Terry, who enjoys taking one of his small fleet of Pony Cycles to shows and events in the Detroit area, either in a large van or in the bed of the 1950s Ford Ranchero he restored. He went on to his own career in tool- and die-making but couldn’t leave the Pony Cycle behind, even though he admits that it represents less of an exciting reminder of the days gone by and more of a “what could have been.” The Pony Cycles in his garage sit next to a few other Hawk Tool & Engineering projects, including a three-wheeled golf cart and sidecar “Pony Car” designed for military use. Of course, there are also a handful of Harley-Davidson motorcycles and a few other projects for good measure. How could someone who grew up in a tool and die operation have it any other way? The post The Pony Cycle’s Short-Lived Success and Lasting Legacy appeared first on Hagerty Media .

title: New Senior Visual Editor for International
body_text: Sergio Peçanha joins the desk as a senior visual editor based in Washington. Read more below from International editor Philip Pan and deputy editor Josh Kelle. We are very happy to announce that Sergio Peçanha has joined the International desk as a senior visual editor based in Washington. Sergio officially returns to The Times to lead graphics and multimedia coverage of the Americas, and he will work across regions to help shape the desk’s broader strategy for visual journalism. Sergio is a multitalented reporter, cartographer and illustrator. As a longtime member of the Graphics department, he produced some of our most distinctive approaches to international stories, including What I Saw in Syria , Walking in War’s Path and The Land That Failed to Fail . He designed a memorable A1 graphic of bin Laden’s compound the day after it was raided, and he collaborated with Metro on Underground Lives and How a Garden for the Poor Became a Playground for the Rich . In 2019, Sergio joined The Washington Post as a graphics columnist and visual editor for the Opinions desk. He created delightful illustrated stories and helped create an editorial series, on how to revive America’s downtowns, that won a Gerald Loeb award for commentary. Earlier this year, Sergio worked on The Times’s Graphics desk in a role focused on editing graphics for reporter video. Sergio began his career at O Globo in his hometown, Rio de Janeiro. He is a generous collaborator who makes the work of his colleagues better. Please welcome Sergio! — Phil and Josh

title: Keeping New Jersey’s gas system safe: Why we’re replacing older gas pipes
summary: Why PSE&G is replacing older gas pipes, relocating some gas meters and investing in infrastructure that serves 1.9 million gas customers in New Jersey. Ever wonder why gas pipes are being replaced in neighborhoods across New Jersey, or why some gas meters are being moved outside? If you’ve noticed construction crews replacing gas pipes in […]
body_text: Why PSE&G is replacing older gas pipes, relocating some gas meters and investing in infrastructure that serves 1.9 million gas customers in New Jersey. Ever wonder why gas pipes are being replaced in neighborhoods across New Jersey, or why some gas meters are being moved outside? If you’ve noticed construction crews replacing gas pipes in your neighborhood or moving gas meters outside homes, you’re seeing work that’s helping keep New Jersey’s gas system safe and reliable. These upgrades help reduce the risk of leaks , strengthen our infrastructure and help ensure safe, dependable natural gas service for the 1.9 million customers who rely on it every day. All while maintaining the lowest residential gas rates in the region for our customers. Through our Gas System Modernization Program (GSMP) , we’ve already replaced more than 1,600 miles of gas mains across New Jersey over the past decade. We’re continuing that progress to help ensure safe, reliable service not only for today but for generations to come. Why are we replacing gas pipes? Because some of the gas pipes serving our communities today are more than 100 years old , replacing them with modern materials helps improve safety, reliability and resiliency. For more than 120 years , we have proudly delivered the energy that keeps your homes warm and bright, businesses running and communities connected across New Jersey. Over that time, we’ve learned a lot about how infrastructure ages and how new technology can help us serve you even better. PSE&G remains the nation’s largest single operator of cast iron gas mains . While those pipes served New Jersey well for decades, older materials are more susceptible to corrosion, cracking and leaks as they age. That’s why we’re replacing older cast iron and unprotected steel pipes with newer, more durable materials designed to improve reliability, reduce leaks and strengthen the safety of the gas system you depend on every day. What does this mean for you, our customers? Once construction is complete, these upgrades may not be visible — but their benefits last for decades. Modernizing our gas system provides lasting benefits, including: Improved safety: Modern pipes and equipment help reduce the risk of leaks. Greater reliability : New infrastructure helps provide more consistent service, including during severe weather. Enhanced resiliency: The upgraded system is better equipped to withstand flooding and other extreme weather. Environmental benefits : Modern pipes help reduce methane emissions while improving system performance. Simply put, these investments help ensure your energy service is dependable today and ready for tomorrow. Why are we relocating gas meters? As part of this modernization work, you may also notice that gas meters are being relocated from inside homes and businesses to outside locations. While this may seem like a small change, it plays an important role in improving safety and service. Moving gas meters outside gives our crews faster access during emergencies, allowing them to safely shut off gas more quickly when necessary. It also reduces the risk of gas building up inside a structure in the event of a leak. Outside meters are also more convenient not only for us, but for you, too. Because our crews can access them without entering your home or business, routine inspections and maintenance are often simpler to schedule while reducing the need for in-home appointments. The ability to complete outside meter inspections also results in long-term cost savings by maximizing operational efficiencies. It’s one more way we’re making New Jersey’s gas system safer while improving service for the people who rely on it every day. How do these upgrades make New Jersey’s gas system more reliable? Energy needs continue to grow, and keeping New Jersey’s gas system strong requires ongoing investment. Natural gas continues to play an important role in providing reliable, affordable energy for homes, businesses and communities across New Jersey, and we continue to maintain the lowest gas bills in the state and region. This reinforces the company’s commitment to providing safe, reliable and cost-effective energy to 1.9 million gas customers across New Jersey and caring for our customers. That’s why we’re continuing to modernize our infrastructure — helping ensure your homes and businesses have safe, reliable natural gas service today and for years to come. Working with our communities We understand that construction can be disruptive, and we don’t take that lightly. That’s why we work closely with communities to keep you informed every step of the way — through mailings, outreach and dedicated project support. If you have questions about construction in your neighborhood, email us at gasworks@pseg.com or visit www.pseg.com/gaswork to learn about current projects and what to expect during construction. Our goal is to be more than just a utility provider. We strive to be a good neighbor and a company you can count on. Looking ahead Our focus is simple: delivering energy that is safe, reliable and dependable . Today and into the future. Every gas main we upgrade and every meter we relocate is an investment in the people and communities we serve, while balancing costs responsibly to provide customers the lowest gas bills in the region. By continuing to modernize New Jersey’s gas system, we’re helping ensure safe, reliable natural gas service for our 1.9 million customers — today and well into the future. title: Wolfspeed and LITEON Partner to Support Hyperscale AI Data Center Deployments with 800 VDC Power Solutions | Wolfspeed
summary: LITEON is collaborating with Wolfspeed to leverage silicon carbide MOSFETs for its next-generation 800 VDC sidecar power platform, targeting leading hyperscale customers and future design opportunities.
body_text: Announcement highlights Wolfspeed and LITEON announce strategic partnership to enable 800 VDC power solutions for next-generation AI data center deployments LITEON is collaborating with Wolfspeed to leverage silicon carbide MOSFETs for its next-generation 800 VDC sidecar power platform, targeting leading hyperscale customers and future design opportunities Leverages Wolfspeed's industry-leading 200mm silicon carbide manufacturing platform to provide supply chain resilience and scalable volume production for AI infrastructure deployments DURHAM, N.C. August 6, 2026 -- Wolfspeed, Inc. (NYSE: WOLF), a global leader in silicon carbide technology, and LITEON Technology Corporation, a leading provider of AI power solutions, today announced a strategic partnership and the successful qualification of Wolfspeed's silicon carbide technology for deployment within LITEON's 800VDC power sidecar and compute rack PSU platforms. These platforms are designed to support next-generation AI data centers for leading hyperscale customers, with the potential for broader adoption across multiple cloud service provider (CSP) platforms and future deployments. AI-driven growth is accelerating the industry's transition to 800 VDC power architectures as data centers prioritize energy efficiency, power density, scalability, and total cost of ownership in critical applications such as power supply units (PSUs) and battery backup units (BBUs). Wolfspeed's family of silicon carbide MOSFETs enables more efficient power delivery across a wide range of operating conditions, helping power system designers maximize efficiency while reducing bill of materials (BOM) costs and simplifying procurement. LITEON is collaborating with Wolfspeed to leverage silicon carbide technology and its 200mm silicon carbide manufacturing platform, in support of hyperscale AI infrastructure deployments. The partnership reflects both companies' commitment to delivering highly reliable 800 VDC power solutions that can be rapidly deployed at scale while meeting the demanding performance and durability requirements of next-generation AI data centers. "Our partnership with LITEON demonstrates Wolfspeed's commitment to enabling the rapidly growing AI data center market through advanced silicon carbide technology and a robust, scalable supply chain," said Robert Feurle, Chief Executive Officer of Wolfspeed. "As hyperscale customers accelerate investments in AI infrastructure, Wolfspeed is uniquely positioned to support the industry's transition to higher-efficiency power architectures." "Integrating Wolfspeed's silicon carbide technology into our 800V VDC power architecture strengthens LITEON's ability to meet the performance, efficiency, and reliability requirements of next-generation AI infrastructure," said John Chang, General Manager, Cloud Infrastructure Platform & Solution SBG, LITEON Technology. " As demand for AI infrastructure continues to accelerate, this collaboration strengthens our ability to support next-generation data center platforms." About Wolfspeed, Inc.
